newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain sees 2.5 pct '98 jobs rise, still many jobless.
newsitem.headline: Spain sees 2.5 pct '98 jobs rise, still many jobless.

text.p: Spain said on Thursday that employment would grow at a rate of 2.5 percent in 1998, but economists said this would not be enough to rein in Europe's highest jobless rate.
Faced with an unemployment rate above 20 percent, twice the European average, Spain's Labour Minister Javier Arenas said he hoped 300,000 new jobs would be created next year.
"With respect to 1998, the forecast (for jobs growth) is for 2.5 percent," Arenas told a news conference. "I believe that in the coming years, (jobs) could grow by more than 300,000 a year."

Some economists said this seemed slightly optimistic, and were sceptical that such growth would succeed in beating down the unemployment rate to below 20 percent, partly because the number of people of working age is rising fast.

"This forecast sounds to be a bit on the high side," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale. "But even if we create these 300,000 jobs next year, the unemployment rate is not going to come down below 20 percent."
Economists forecast that average unemployment for the year would remain around 20.25 to 20.6 percent.
On Wednesday, Spain's National Statistics Institute (INE) said unemployment fell to 20.94 percent in the second quarter from 21.29 percent in the first, according to a household survey.
While Spain's one-year-old conservative government has made great strides in shaking up the economy for the launch of Europe's single currency, unemployment remains a thorn in its side.
In an effort to tackle the problem, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar vowed 1997 would be the year of the job and pledged to create 200,000 new jobs.
The economy is performing better than expected, and job creation is expected to exceed that figure this year.

Economists said the dramatic growth in the working population is disguising a better job-creation trend than unemployment numbers suggest, and is one reason why the unemployment rate will not fall below 20 percent until 1999.

"A jobs growth of 2.5 percent in 1997 means an increase in employment of just over 300,000 people and in that case unemployment would fall by slightly more than 100,000," said Jose Luis Alzola, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.
"This will mean an average unemployment rate of around 20.6 percent," he added.
Economists said reforms introduced in May and aimed at modernising Spain's rigid labour market would help to create more stability but were unlikely to touch the swollen unemployment rate.
A shift from temporary to permanent contracts since the reforms came into effect are the first signs of such stability.
The Labour Ministry forecast that permanent contracts would account for 9.4 percent of all contracts in July compared with just 3.2 percent a year earlier.
"There has been some shift from temporary jobs to permanent jobs. But whether the labour reforms are helping to increase employment more than otherwise - I doubt it," said Alzola.
